criteria.descriptor: Full marks: every mechanism cited is correct and correctly applied — pinning dated snapshots vs floating aliases, DPA / training opt-out / zero-retention / data residency, PII redaction, regression evals with judge+human review, feature-flag/canary/shadow rollout with rollback. No false claims (e.g. that the retired snapshot can be kept forever, that a newer model is a guaranteed upgrade, or that client-side deletion controls vendor retention). Deduct for each inaccurate or misapplied control.

Full marks: substantively covers all four required areas — (1) versioning & forced-deprecation handling, (2) pre-cutover evaluation, (3) data/contractual controls, (4) safe rollout with monitoring and rollback — plus inventory/registry and vendor lock-in/fallback. Deduct proportionally for each area missing or treated only superficially.

Full marks: justifies the key trade-offs — why pin instead of track latest, why re-evaluate rather than trust 'newer is better', why staged rollout over a hard cutover, and the privacy-vs-utility tension of redaction — rather than listing controls. Partial credit for some justification; little credit for an unreasoned checklist.

Full marks: organised, uses correct governance/LLM-ops vocabulary (model registry, DPA, ZDR/zero-retention, canary/shadow, guardrail metrics, rollback), and reads as a coherent plan a reviewer could act on. Deduct for disorganised, vague, or jargon-without-meaning writing.

expected_answer_points: Pin explicit dated model snapshots and never rely on a floating 'latest'/default alias; the vendor's auto-migration is an uncontrolled change that must be gated, and the migration must be completed within the deprecation window since the old snapshot cannot be kept indefinitely
Maintain a model inventory/registry (model, version, provider, purpose, owner, approval, model card, audit trail) so third-party models are governed like internal ones

Run the candidate model against a versioned regression/eval suite (golden + adversarial cases, task metrics, LLM-as-judge and human review) comparing quality, latency, cost and safety/refusal behaviour — do not assume newer is better because of behavioural/prompt drift
Establish data-handling and contractual controls: a DPA, opt-out of training on your data, zero/limited data retention, data residency, and PII minimisation/redaction before sending customer data
Verify and document what data crosses the trust boundary and that retention/training terms hold for the new model/endpoint (terms can differ per model)

Operate a safe rollout: feature-flag the model choice, shadow/canary or A/B while keeping the old snapshot live, with guardrail metrics, alerting, and an instant rollback path (previous snapshot or fallback provider)
Use a provider/model abstraction and a fallback model to reduce single-vendor lock-in, and continue monitoring for drift after cutover
common_pitfalls: Assumes the vendor's newer default is a strict upgrade and swaps without a regression eval, ignoring behavioural drift, formatting changes, refusal-rate shifts, and prompt sensitivity
Treats the change as a routine code deploy and omits the data-privacy/contractual dimension entirely (no DPA, no training opt-out, no retention/residency check)

Leaves production pointed at a floating 'latest'/default alias — the very thing that caused the surprise auto-migration — or proposes to keep using the retired snapshot indefinitely with no migration plan inside the window
Offers only prompt tweaks or temperature changes and never addresses versioning, an inventory/registry, monitoring, or rollback
Says 'we'll test it' without a concrete eval set, guardrail metrics, or a staged canary/shadow rollout and rollback path
Believes redacting or deleting data client-side controls what the vendor retains, instead of relying on contractual zero-retention/no-training terms, and ignores single-vendor lock-in / fallback
reference_answer:
I treat the hosted model as an external dependency under change control, not a static building block.

Versioning & deprecation: I always pin explicit dated snapshots and never point production at a floating 'latest'/default alias — the auto-migration is exactly the uncontrolled change I want to prevent. I record the model, provider, version, purpose, owner, and approval in a model inventory/registry alongside a model card, so third-party models are governed like internal ones. Since a retired snapshot can't be kept forever, I plan the migration inside the 90-day window rather than being force-cut, and use a provider/model abstraction layer so the model id is a config value, reducing lock-in and letting me keep a fallback provider.

Validation before cutover: newer is not automatically better — models drift in behaviour, formatting, refusal rates and prompt sensitivity. I run the candidate against a versioned regression suite: a golden set of representative and adversarial support cases scored with task metrics plus LLM-as-judge and human spot-checks, and I compare quality, latency, cost, and safety/refusal behaviour against the incumbent. Prompts and few-shot examples may need re-tuning for the new model.

Data & contractual controls: I confirm a signed DPA, opt out of training on our data, and enable zero-/limited-retention (enterprise) terms; I verify data residency and document exactly what data crosses the trust boundary. I minimise and redact PII (names, emails, order ids) before the call where feasible, and log that the boundary and retention posture were re-verified for the new model — vendor terms can differ by model or endpoint.

Safe switch: I gate the model behind a feature flag, run shadow/canary or an A/B split so the old snapshot stays live, and define guardrail metrics (quality, latency p95, cost/req, error and escalation rates) with alerting. If guardrails breach, I roll back to the previous snapshot or fallback provider instantly. After cutover I keep monitoring for drift and re-run evals on any provider-side change.
